# Write a skill {#sec-skills}

Every lab has checks that live in someone's head. Before anyone plots a DESeq2 table,
the person who has been burned before asks which group is the reference. Before a
sample sheet goes to the core, someone looks for the duplicated row and the three date
formats. Before a qPCR plate gets analysed, someone checks the no-template controls.
None of this is written down, so it gets done when that person is in the room and
forgotten when they're not. An agent has the same problem: each new session starts
knowing nothing about your lab's traps, and you end up explaining them again, or,
worse, not explaining them and getting a confident answer that skipped the check that
mattered.

A **skill** is how you write a check like that down once, in a form an agent picks up
by itself when the task calls for it. It's a folder with a Markdown file in it. No
code, no build step, no registration. The file says what the procedure is for, when
to use it, and what to do, and the agent loads it when your request matches.

The part people don't expect is who does the writing. **You don't write the skill by
hand. The agent writes it, with your direction, and you verify it.** Your contribution
is the part the agent can't supply: what a good file looks like, which problems you've
actually seen, which of them lead to wrong conclusions, and what the skill must never
do. The agent is good at turning that into a clear, well-structured instruction file.
It's bad at knowing that your core's exports put the plate barcode in row 3, and it
can't know whether its own skill works until you test it on a file where you already
know the answer. This chapter is about that division of labour.

## What you'll learn

- What a skill is, where it lives, and how an agent decides to load one.
- What a published library of scientific skills offers, and what its own authors say
  it doesn't show.
- How to read a real skill, `deseq2-triage`, and why each part of it is there.
- What a skill changes, by comparing the same request with it and without it.
- How to direct an agent to write a skill for a file *you* check often.
- How to verify it: on a good file, on a file with problems you planted, and on the
  wording that should (and shouldn't) make it load.

## What a skill is

A skill is a folder whose name is the skill's name, containing a file called
`SKILL.md` (@fig-skills-folder). The file starts with a short header, between two
`---` lines, holding two fields: `name` and `description`. Everything after the
header is instructions, written in plain Markdown, for the agent to follow. A skill
can also carry `scripts/` (code for the agent to run) and `references/` (longer
documents it reads only when a step says to), but many good skills are a single file.

![A skill is a folder. Only `SKILL.md` is required; the rest is optional. The folder
sits in `.claude/skills/` inside a project, or in your home folder to be available
everywhere.](../images/skills-folder.svg){#fig-skills-folder fig-alt="Folder tree:
my-analysis contains .claude, which contains skills, which contains deseq2-triage.
Inside it, SKILL.md is required; README.md is for people; scripts and references
folders are optional."}

### The description decides everything

When a session starts, the agent doesn't read your skills. It reads a list of their
names and descriptions: a line or two each. Only when your request matches a
description does it load the rest of that skill's file (@fig-skills-loading). This is
called **progressive disclosure**, and it's why you can have dozens of skills without
filling the agent's memory: the instructions cost nothing until they're needed
[@url:https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-skills-loading
%%| fig-cap: "How a skill gets loaded. The agent sees only the description until your
%%|   request matches it. A skill whose description never matches never runs, and
%%|   nothing tells you."
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart: the session starts; the agent reads each skill's name and
%%|   description; if your request matches one, it loads the full SKILL.md and any
%%|   files the steps point to; if not, it answers without the skill."
flowchart LR
  accDescr: Flowchart - the session starts, the agent reads each skill's name and
  A["Session starts"] --> B["Agent reads every skill's<br/>name and description"]
  B --> C{"Does your request<br/>match a description?"}
  C -- "no" --> D["Answers without it<br/>(no warning)"]
  C -- "yes" --> E["Loads the full SKILL.md,<br/>then scripts/ or references/<br/>only if a step says to"]
```

The consequence is the most important fact in this chapter. The agent never sees the
body of a skill until it has already decided to use it, so **a skill that never loads
is indistinguishable from a skill you never wrote**. No error, no warning: you just
get the answer you'd have got anyway. A good description says what the skill does,
then when to use it, in the words you'd actually type: "check", "sanity-check", "is
this OK", "can I trust this".

### Where skills live

::: {.column-margin}
**An open format.** `SKILL.md` follows the Agent Skills standard
[@url:https://agentskills.io], so the same folder works in Codex CLI, Google Antigravity
and GitHub Copilot as well as Claude Code. Where each tool looks for skills differs
(Antigravity: `.agents/skills/` in the project); check its documentation.
:::

| Where | Path | Who gets it |
|:---|:---|:---|
| This project | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, inside the folder you start the agent in | Anyone working in this folder; share it with the folder |
| Just you, everywhere | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, in your home folder | You, in every project on this computer |

: Where Claude Code looks for skills. Start with the project folder: it keeps the
skill next to the data it's for, and it's easy to find and delete. Source: the Claude
Code skills documentation. {#tbl-skills-where}

In the Claude desktop app, type `/` in the prompt box to see the skills available in a
session, or ask the agent "What skills are available?". Both are useful for checking
that a new skill was found at all.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## On Windows

- `~` means your home folder, `C:\Users\<you>`. So personal skills live in
  `C:\Users\<you>\.claude\skills\`. Project skills live in `.claude\skills\` inside
  your project folder.
- Folders whose names start with a dot can be awkward to create by hand in File
  Explorer. Let the agent create them: "save it as `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in
  this folder" works the same on Windows and macOS.
- If a skill runs scripts, prefer Python or R over shell scripts. A skill that needs
  `bash` fails on Windows unless Git for Windows is installed.

More in @sec-windows.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Can't see `.claude` on a Mac?
Finder hides folders whose names start with a dot. Press **Cmd + Shift + .** in a
Finder window to show them, and again to hide them.
:::

### What makes a good skill

The best skills encode knowledge that **isn't in the data**. An agent can read a table
perfectly well; what it can't know is the thing your lab learned the hard way. Ask of
any candidate procedure: would a careful newcomer, with the file in front of them,
work this out? If yes, the agent probably will too, and the skill adds little. If no
(which group is the reference, which instrument column is unreliable, which sample
names break the join) it's worth a skill.

Skills and the `AGENTS.md` file from @sec-teach do different jobs. `AGENTS.md` holds
the **rules** for one project, read at the start of every session there. A skill holds
a **procedure**, loaded only when a task needs it, in whichever project you're in. When
a section of your `AGENTS.md` has turned into a list of steps, it wants to be a skill.

## Skills someone else wrote {#sec-skills-library}

You don't have to write every skill yourself. One large open collection for science is
[Scientific Agent Skills](https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills),
from the company K-Dense: 166 skills when we looked on 23 September 2026, MIT-licensed,
covering genomics, single-cell, cheminformatics, imaging, statistics, study design and
scientific writing. It uses the same open format as this chapter, so its skills work in
Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex and others. Several sit close to this chapter's worked
example: `pydeseq2` (running a DESeq2 analysis in Python), `bulk-rnaseq` (from reads to
differential expression), `experimental-design` and `statistical-analysis`.

The team also wrote a paper about it [@doi:10.48550/arXiv.2609.00065]
(@fig-skills-ksk-paper), and it's worth reading for two reasons. The first is its
opening, which lists the mistakes an agent makes when it writes code that runs but an
analysis that isn't defensible: no multiple-testing correction, a hundred cells from
each of three mice counted as three hundred replicates, a BED file's zero-based start
read as one-based. Each is answered by a rule in one of the skills. The
`experimental-design` skill, for instance, says that "3 mice with 100 cells each is
n = 3 (mice), not n = 300 (cells)". That's what a good skill holds: a procedural fact
the field agrees on and an agent won't reliably apply unprompted.

::: {.column-margin}
![The first page of the paper: sixteen areas of practice, and what's inside a skill's
folder. CC BY 4.0, Kassis et al.
(2026).](../images/skills-ksk-paper.png){#fig-skills-ksk-paper fig-alt="First page of
the arXiv paper 'Scientific Agent Skills: A Library of Procedural Knowledge for Research
Agents' by Kassis, Agarwal, He, Patel and Brueckner of K-Dense. A figure shows sixteen
tiles for areas of scientific practice, such as genomics, single-cell omics and
statistics and study design, next to a diagram of a skill directory: instruction file,
reference documents, executable scripts, static assets and versioned metadata. The
abstract is below."}
:::

The second reason is rarer: the paper is candid about what it hasn't shown. Its
abstract says: "We report no task-level evaluation and no host selection rate." Its
limitations section is, in effect, a list of this chapter's warnings, measured on a
library of 163 skills (@tbl-skills-paper).

| The paper reports | This chapter's point |
|---|---|
| No test of whether the skills improve an agent's work: "Skills structure scientific judgment; they do not replace expert review" | A skill is a claim until you've tested it on a file where you know the answer |
| No measure of how often an agent picks the right skill. They could only compare descriptions' wording; the closest pair is two chemistry toolkits | The description decides everything, and a skill that never loads fails silently |
| "A selected skill can still fail scientifically": the agent may skip steps or load only part of it | Check the output, not just that the skill loaded |
| The descriptions of all 163 skills take up 7.1% of a 200,000-token context window before any of them is used. They recommend installing only what a project needs | Every installed skill costs context in every session |
| 32 of 163 skills don't list the team as author, and community skills may get less review. Skills can run code | Read a `SKILL.md` before you install it |

: What the Scientific Agent Skills paper says about itself, and the matching point in
this chapter. The paper describes release v2.65.0. {#tbl-skills-paper}

A library can't hold your lab's knowledge. The `pydeseq2` skill knows how to *run*
DESeq2, carefully. It can't know that the two Vahedi lab tables in the worked example
below use opposite fold-change conventions, because that isn't a fact about DESeq2;
it's a fact about these files. Use a library for the procedures a whole field shares,
and write your own for what only your lab knows.

::: {.callout-note}
## For discussion

1. The authors say they haven't tested whether the skills help. Would you install one
   anyway? What would you want to see first, and could you run that test yourself, on
   one skill, in an afternoon?
2. Would your agent get "3 mice with 100 cells each is n = 3" right *without* the skill?
   How would you find out? (The paper warns that if a strong model already gets a task
   right, a test can't show a skill helping.)
3. The repository describes itself as "used by 190,000+ scientists worldwide". The paper
   says its installation estimate "counts clients that fetch the library, not scientists
   or sessions in which an agent used a skill", and that "Reach is not use". Which statement would you quote in a grant?
4. How many skills would you install before the standing cost outweighed the benefit?
   Who in your lab would review a skill before everyone uses it?
5. Which of your lab's checks will never be in a public library?
:::

## Worked example: `deseq2-triage`

This workshop's repository includes a skill,
[`deseq2-triage`](https://github.com/seandavi/2026-penn-epigen-agentic-workshop/tree/main/examples/skills/deseq2-triage),
written for the two DESeq2 results tables in the
[Vahedi lab's workshop repository](https://github.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop)
(`track-a/data/`). DESeq2 [@doi:10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8] results tables arrive
without the facts you need to read them: the genome build, the coordinate
convention, which group is the reference, and what was filtered before export. The
numbers are fine. The context is missing.

The two tables make the point sharply. The data README says that in
`differential_genes.tsv` a positive fold change means *higher in wild type* (lower in
the knockout), while in `differential_peaks.csv` it means *more H3K27ac in the
knockout*. The two files use opposite conventions, and neither says so.

### Reading the skill, part by part

Open
[`SKILL.md`](https://github.com/seandavi/2026-penn-epigen-agentic-workshop/blob/main/examples/skills/deseq2-triage/SKILL.md)
alongside this table. Each part is there for a reason.

| Part | What it says | Why it's there |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `name` | `deseq2-triage` | Matches the folder name. Lowercase, hyphens. |
| `description` | What it checks, then "Use when the user asks to check, QC, sanity-check, triage, or look over a results table … or asks what is wrong with one or whether it can be trusted." | This is what the agent matches your request against. It lists the words people actually use. |
| What this is for | The four missing facts. "Run these checks and report. Do not fix anything." | Tells the agent the *goal*, so it can handle a table that doesn't fit the steps exactly. |
| Step 2, direction | Work the direction out from the per-sample counts if they're there. If not, report `UNVERIFIABLE`. "Do not infer it from column order, from group names … Do not guess." | The trap that matters most, and the one an agent is most tempted to paper over. Forbidding the specific guesses is what stops them. |
| Steps 3–6 | Missing `padj`, p-values of exactly 0, chromosome names, interval widths, duplicated IDs | The lab's known traps, each with the reason it matters (a naive filter drops rows; `-log10(0)` is infinity; `chr1` never joins to `1`). |
| Step 7, report | Three sections: **Blocking**, **Worth knowing**, **Checked and fine**, then the four facts to ask for | A fixed shape makes reports comparable from one file to the next, and puts what stops you first. |
| Constraints | Report only; don't write a cleaned copy; don't state a direction you haven't shown from counts; stop | Agents are helpful. Without these, it may "fix" the table and carry on to a volcano plot. |

: The parts of `deseq2-triage/SKILL.md`. The
[README](https://github.com/seandavi/2026-penn-epigen-agentic-workshop/blob/main/examples/skills/deseq2-triage/README.md)
beside it is for people: why the skill exists, and how to install it. The agent
doesn't need it. {#tbl-skills-parts}

Two lessons carry over to any skill you write. First, **the "don't" lines matter as
much as the steps**: each one closes off a helpful-looking move that would destroy
the point of the check. Second, **say why**. "Count rows where `padj` is missing"
gets you a number; adding "a naive `padj < 0.05` filter silently discards those rows"
gets you a warning a person will act on.

### Running it

We ran it on 23 September 2026. We made an empty folder, copied the skill into
`.claude/skills/deseq2-triage/`, downloaded the two tables, and asked Claude Code
(Claude Opus 5.5) about each file in a fresh session. The prompt deliberately doesn't
name the skill:

```default
I've been handed differential_peaks.csv by a collaborator. Can I trust it?
Sanity-check it before I use it.
```

Both times, the agent loaded `deseq2-triage` on its own: "sanity-check" and "can I
trust it" are in the description. Here is the start of its report on the peaks file,
unedited apart from shortening:

> **Blocking**
>
> 1. **Fold-change direction: can't be checked from this file.** Without per-sample
>    counts, nothing here shows which group a positive `log2FoldChange` means. The
>    reference level has to come from the analyst or their DESeq2 script […] If the
>    direction is wrong, every "gained" peak is really a "lost" one.
>
> **Worth knowing**
>
> 2. **No missing `padj` values, which suggests the table was filtered before
>    export.** […]
> 3. **4 rows have `pvalue` and `padj` exactly 0.** That's floating-point underflow,
>    not certainty. On a volcano plot `-log10(0)` is infinity […]
> 4. **Chromosome names use the Ensembl style (`1`, `2`, …, `X`, `Y`), not UCSC
>    (`chr1`).** Joining against a UCSC-style file […] will match nothing, and it
>    won't raise an error.

On the genes file, it worked the direction out from the counts: "positive
`log2FoldChange` means higher in WT than in CTCFBSKO", consistent for all 60
significant genes, with *Jun* as the worked case. It flagged that 20,982 genes have no
adjusted p-value, and explained that they are "not tested", not "not significant".
That's DESeq2's independent filtering [@doi:10.1073/pnas.0914005107].

**We didn't take the report on trust.** We recounted every number in it with a short
script (rows, missing `padj`, zero p-values, the 60/60 direction check, the 16
duplicated gene symbols, the widths from 180 to 93,567 bp) and compared the findings
with the quirks listed in the Vahedi lab's
[data README](https://github.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/blob/main/track-a/data/README.md).
All matched.

### The same question, without the skill

A skill is only worth having if it changes something. So we asked the same question,
about the same files, in a folder with no skill (@tbl-skills-compare).

| Known problem (from the data README) | File | With the skill | Without it |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Positive fold change means higher in WT | genes | **Blocking**; shown from counts, 60/60 | Found from counts; its first concern |
| `padj` missing for 20,982 genes | genes | **Blocking**; "not tested", not "not significant" | Found; also "not tested" |
| 16 duplicated gene symbols | genes | Worth knowing: join on `Gene_ID` | Mentioned as normal |
| Direction unstated, no counts to check it | peaks | **Blocking**: `UNVERIFIABLE` | Half a sentence at the end of another point |
| 4 p-values of exactly 0 (underflow) | peaks | Worth knowing | **Not mentioned** |
| No `chr` prefix | peaks | Worth knowing: joins fail silently | Mentioned |
| Widths up to 93,567 bp | peaks | Worth knowing | "Minor" |
| Time taken | both | 48 s and 43 s | 91 s and 90 s |

: One run of each, same model, same prompt, on 23 September 2026. Agents vary from
run to run, so treat this as an illustration, not a benchmark. {#tbl-skills-compare}

The agent without the skill wasn't careless. It did a lot: it reported recomputing
the p-values and the Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment (we didn't check that), and it
noticed that three peaks on chromosome Y are strongly up. (We checked: they
are.) But it chose its own checks, so it skipped one the lab knows matters
(underflow). It buried the one that matters most for the peaks file (direction). And
its explanation for the Y peaks, that "the two groups contain different numbers of
males", can't be right as stated: the data README says these samples come from a
**cell line**. The agent didn't know that, because the file doesn't say.

That's the case for a skill in one table. **Without it, you get a thoughtful answer
that varies with the agent's choices. With it, you get your lab's checks, every
time, in the same order, and it stops when it's done.**

## Your turn: create your own

You'll direct an agent to write a skill that checks a kind of file you handle often,
then verify it. Budget 30–40 minutes. @fig-skills-loop shows who does what.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-skills-loop
%%| fig-cap: "Writing a skill with an agent. You supply what the agent can't know, and
%%|   you do the testing; the agent does the writing."
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart: you describe the file and its traps; the agent interviews you
%%|   and drafts SKILL.md; you read the draft and test it on a good file, a bad file,
%%|   and the words that should load it; if anything fails, the agent revises and you
%%|   test again; if all pass, you keep it."
flowchart TD
  accDescr: Flowchart - you describe the file and its traps, the agent interviews you
  A["<b>You</b>: the file, what good looks like,<br/>the traps you've seen"] --> B["<b>Agent</b>: interviews you,<br/>drafts SKILL.md"]
  B --> C["<b>You</b>: read the draft; test it on a good file,<br/>a file with planted problems,<br/>and the words that should load it"]
  C -- "something failed" --> D["<b>Agent</b>: revises,<br/>from what you found"]
  D --> C
  C -- "all passed" --> E["Keep it"]
```

### 1. Pick a file you check by hand

Your own material first. Good candidates are files that arrive from somewhere else
and have burned you before (@tbl-skills-ideas).

| File | The checks you might already do in your head |
|:---|:---|
| A sample sheet for the sequencing core | Duplicate IDs, inconsistent names, mixed date formats, missing conditions, characters the pipeline rejects |
| A qPCR export | No-template controls amplified, replicate Ct spread, missing wells, undetermined values |
| A peak file (BED, narrowPeak) | `chr` prefix, 0- or 1-based starts, zero-width peaks, genome build |
| A FastQC or MultiQC summary | Failed modules that matter for your assay versus ones that don't |
| A flow cytometry or plate-reader export | Units, blank wells, saturated values, the plate layout |

: Candidate files for a checking skill. {#tbl-skills-ideas}

**No file of your own to hand?** Use the Vahedi lab's
[`sample_sheet_messy.csv`](https://github.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/blob/main/track-a/data/sample_sheet_messy.csv),
a simulated RNA-seq submission sheet with known problems. (Their afternoon has an
exercise that *cleans* this sheet. Here you're writing a skill that *checks* sheets
like it and fixes nothing.) Or extend `deseq2-triage` with a trap from your own lab's
pipeline.

To use the fallback, once you've made the `skill` folder and started a session on it
(step 2), ask the agent to fetch the exact file rather than retype it:

```default
Download this file into this folder, saving it byte for byte (curl on macOS,
Invoke-WebRequest on Windows), not by retyping it:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/main/track-a/data/sample_sheet_messy.csv
Then tell me how many rows and columns it has.
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Privacy: what you show the agent leaves your computer
Anything the agent reads is sent to the model. Use a file you'd be allowed to email
to a collaborator: no patient data, nothing identifiable, and nothing unpublished
that your lab's rules keep in-house. For a sensitive file type, describe it in words
and make a small fake example.
:::

### 2. Have the agent interview you

Make a folder called `skill` inside `Documents/agents-workshop/`, put a copy of your
example file in it (or fetch the fallback, above), and start a **new** session on that
folder, as in [Setup](00-setup.qmd). Then paste this, filling in the angle brackets:

```default
I want you to write a skill (a SKILL.md in the Agent Skills format) that checks
<a kind of file, e.g. "the sample sheets we send to our sequencing core"> before
anyone uses it. There's an example in this folder: <file name>.

Don't write anything yet. First interview me, one question at a time, about:
- where these files come from, and what a good one looks like;
- the problems I've actually seen in them, and which would lead to a wrong result;
- anything that can't be checked from the file alone and must be asked of a person;
- what the skill must never do (for example, change the file);
- the words I'd use when asking for this check.

Then show me a draft. The skill must report problems, not fix them, and must say
plainly when something can't be checked from the file. Save it to
.claude/skills/<short-name>/SKILL.md in this folder only when I say it's right.
```

Answer from experience. The most useful answers are specific: not "check the dates"
but "we've had three date formats in one sheet, and `3/2/26` means 3 February to our
UK collaborators".

### 3. Read the draft before you accept it

It's short; read all of it. Check that:

- the **description** says what it does, then when to use it, in your words;
- every trap you mentioned is there, **with the reason it matters**;
- there's a **"do not"** for each helpful-looking move you don't want (fixing the
  file, filling in missing values, carrying on to an analysis);
- the report has a fixed shape, with what stops you first;
- it doesn't claim to check something it can't. Ask the agent: "Which of these checks
  could give a wrong answer, and how would I know?"

Ask for changes in plain language. Then let it save the file.

### 4. Test it on a file where you know the answer

Testing is your job, not the agent's. It needs two files.

1. **A good file.** A real one you've already checked by hand. The skill should report
   little or nothing, and nothing false.
2. **A bad file.** Copy the good one and break it yourself: add a duplicate row,
   delete a value, change one date format, misspell a sample name. **Write down what
   you broke before you run the check.** Then you know exactly what it should find.

Run each in a **new session**, so the agent that wrote the skill can't answer from
memory, with a prompt that doesn't name the skill:

```default
I've just been sent <file name>. Is it OK to use?
```

Compare what it reports with your list. Anything missed means the instructions need
work. Anything it invented is worse: tell the agent exactly what it claimed, and ask
it to change the skill so that can't happen again.

### 5. Test the description

Now test the part that decides whether the skill ever runs. Write three requests that
**should** load it and three neighbouring ones that **shouldn't**. Use how you'd
really ask, not how you'd describe the skill.

| Should load it | Should *not* load it |
|:---|:---|
| "Can you look over this sample sheet?" | "Make me a blank sample sheet template" |
| "Is this ready to send to the core?" | "What does the core charge per lane?" |
| "Anything wrong with tconv_batch2.csv?" | "Plot the harvest dates in this sheet" |

: An example should/shouldn't pair for a sample-sheet checker. {#tbl-skills-triggers}

Try each in a new session. If you can't tell from the transcript whether the skill
was used, ask "Did you use a skill for that?". When a phrasing you'd genuinely use
doesn't load it, tell the agent the phrase and ask it to revise the description, then
test again. The usual failure is a skill that loads too rarely, not too often, so
lean towards a description with more of your everyday words in it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If it never loads at all
Ask "What skills are available?". If yours isn't listed, the folder is in the wrong
place, or the header between the `---` lines is malformed. Ask the agent to check
both. You can always run a skill directly by typing `/` and its name.
:::

## What to notice

- **You wrote almost none of it,** and it still encodes exactly what you know. The
  value was in your answers and your tests, not the typing.
- **The "do not" lines did real work.** Without them, a checking skill drifts into a
  fixing skill, and a fixed file hides the problem you most needed to see.
- **The agent can't verify its own skill.** It can check that the file is well formed.
  Only a file where you know the answer tells you whether the checks are right.
- **The description is an interface.** It failed silently or it worked; there was no
  error message either way.

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-tip}
## You're done when

- [ ] Your skill is at `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in your project folder.
- [ ] On your good file, it reported nothing false.
- [ ] On your broken file, it found everything you planted, or you've changed it so it
      does.
- [ ] It loaded for a phrasing that isn't copied from its description, and didn't load
      for a neighbouring request.
- [ ] You've added a ledger entry (@sec-ledger) saying what you tested it on and what
      it missed.
:::

## Going further

- **Real examples.** Anthropic's
  [life-sciences](https://github.com/anthropics/life-sciences) repository publishes
  skills for scientific work. Read
  [`single-cell-rna-qc`](https://github.com/anthropics/life-sciences/tree/main/single-cell-rna-qc):
  a `SKILL.md` that runs Python scripts from `scripts/` and reads scverse QC guidance
  from `references/` only when needed. It's the same format you just used, grown
  larger.
- **Try a library skill, one at a time.** To try one skill from Scientific Agent Skills
  (@sec-skills-library) in a project, read its `SKILL.md` on GitHub first, then ask:

  ```default
  Download only the pydeseq2 skill from https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills (the folder skills/pydeseq2, with everything in it) into .claude/skills/pydeseq2 in this folder. Don't install anything else, and don't run any of its scripts. If git isn't available, download the files one by one. Then list the files you saved and show me the header of its SKILL.md.
  ```

  The repository's README describes installers for the whole collection. Its own
  security advice is not to install everything at once.
- **Share it with your lab.** A skill in a project's `.claude/skills/` travels with
  the project. Put it in a shared lab folder or repository (@sec-project), and every
  trainee who starts there gets your checks without having to know they exist.
- **Measure it.** The `skill-creator` plugin for Claude Code runs a skill against test
  prompts with and without it, and suggests description changes. See "Evaluate and
  iterate on a skill" in the skills documentation
  [@url:https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills].
- **Connect it to data.** Skills tell an agent *how*; MCP servers (@sec-mcp) give it
  access to databases it can't otherwise reach. The two combine.
